CRYSTAL OSCILLATORE
Crystal oscillators use a component called a crystal (XTAL).
DISCUSSION
The crystals of certain materials, such as quartz, have natural oscillation frequencies.
A rectangular slab of crystal is cut and placed between two metal plates to form a crystal oscillator.
Crystals are useful because they exhibit the piezoelectric effect. That is, they vibrate when voltage is applied and they produce AC voltage at the output..
The frequency of the vibrations is equal to the frequency of the AC voltage. For our discussion, this is the resonant frequency.
the cut of crystal (k) and the thickness (t) of crystal slab.
The resonant frequency of a crystal oscillator is determined by the cut of crystal (k) and the thickness (t) of crystal slab.
The constant, K, depends on different piezoelectric properties of the crystal.
Fortunately, you do not have to calculate the resonant frequency of crystals. It is printed on the component housing.t.
The value stamped on the crystal is very accurate, with little tolerance.
You may have noticed the similarity in construction of the crystal and a capacitor.
The crystal does have a very small amount of capacitance known as mounting capacitance (Cm).
With this in mind, let's look at a common crystal oscillator circuit.
There are many different types of crystal oscillators. This is a variation of a MOSFET Pierce Crystal Oscillator.
It is identified as a crystal oscillator by the crystal in the feedback circuit.
Notice the reference designator "Y" for a crystal.
Q1 is the amplifier. It is a dual gate, N channel, depletion type field effect transistor (MOSFET).
FETs are commonly used in crystal oscillators because they offer simplistic design requirements.
The number of biasing components is reduced. R1 is the gate return resistor. It supplies the ground or zero volt reference for the gate.
An AC signal on the gate will increase and decrease drain current.
Self bias is developed across the source resistor R2. The FET operates as a class A amplifier.
L1 is an RF choke that appears as a open to AC, isolating the supply from the circuit while functioning as a drain load resistor for VDD.
C2 is a coupling capacitor, isolating the DC operating voltage from the output.
R3 is the output load resistor, providing variable amplitude for the output signal.
As soon as VDD is applied to the circuit, the crystal begins to vibrate. The piezoelectric effect causes Y1 to produce a small AC voltage.
The frequency of the AC is the natural frequency of the crystal. The signal is applied to both gates of the amplifier.
The amplified signal on the drain is inverted. This provides 180 degrees of phase shift.
The amplified, inverted signal is applied to the other side of the crystal.
This signal keeps the crystal vibrating and sustains oscillations. The AC produced by the crystal is inverted. This is regenerative feedback.
The mounting capacitance of the crystal (Cm) and C1 form a voltage divider to limit the amount of feedback.
Correct operation is determined by comparing the value of the crystal with the actual measured frequency.

NORMAL OPERATION OF A CRYSTAL OSCILLATOR - Determine the normal operating frequency of a crystal oscillator by observing the value printed on the crystal housing. Compare this frequency with the measured frequency.
The resonant frequency of crystal oscillators is very accurate. The frequency does not drift as it does in LC and RC oscillators.

DRIFT - Drift is an unwanted condition in oscillators that causes the frequency to change. It is present to some extent in all oscillators but is very small in crystal oscillators. Some clocks using crystal oscillators take 300 years to gain or lose 1 second.
DEFINITION
Drift is caused by temperature changes, aging, and other factors. Oscillators with small drift are said to have good stability.
Many electronic timing devices use crystal oscillators because of their excellent stability.
